newsitem.title: USA: Thousands urge protection of ancient U.S. redwoods.
newsitem.headline: Thousands urge protection of ancient U.S. redwoods.

text.p: Several thousand people held a colorful and noisy rally near America's largest privately-owned ancient redwood forest on Sunday to protest plans by a timber company to harvest some trees.

News reports said singer Bonnie Raitt was among more than 300 people arrested at the northern California protest for trespassing on the property of Pacific Lumber Co. -- owner of Headwaters forest -- in an act of civil disobedience.
Those arrested were cited and released.
"What we are doing here today is reaffirming our commitment to protecting what is left of this fantastic ancient-growth resource that we have," Raitt told reporters.

The crowd, unofficially estimated at 3,000, gathered near the small town of Carlotta, 250 miles (400 kms) north of San Francisco, to demand that Headwaters forest be permanently protected from logging.
The environmentalists' demonstration was planned for Sunday because Pacific Lumber Co. has a permit to begin "salvage logging" in the forest on Monday.
The permit allows the company to remove dead, dying and diseased trees from Headwaters, although the company said it would only remove fallen trees. The giant redwoods are worth up to $50,000 each.

The Clinton administration and officials from Pacific Lumber's parent company, MAXXAM Inc, have been holding intensive negotiations in Washington to seek a solution to the dispute. They are discussing a possible exchange of the forest for surplus federal land or rights to harvest trees on other federal land, officials said.
No agreement has been reached but Pacific Lumber agreed last Friday not to harvest redwoods in the forest for the next two weeks to allow time for negotiations.

"Save Headwaters now", chanted the demonstrators, some waving flags and signs with slogans such as "Let them live." One demonstrator wore a tree mask and a motorcyclist wore a spotted owl costume. Sheriff's deputies with riot helmets kept watch on the crowd, which also included Eagles rock band singer Don Henley.
Sheriff's officials could not immediately be reached for comment.

Environmentalists say the 3,000-acre grove and several other redwood stands in the area provide vital habitat for endangered species such as the marbled murrelet. Environmental groups have fought for years to prevent any logging in the forest.
In nearby Eureka, a counter-demonstration was held by lumber industry supporters who drove logging trucks through the town.
Mary Bullwinkel, a spokeswoman for Pacific Lumber, said the environmentalists' demonstration "doesn't really provide any positive contribution to resolving the issue."
